Horror is the genre parents worry about least -- and should worry about most. The anxiety is usually about gore: how much blood, how many jump scares, whether the kid can sleep afterward. But gore washes off. The real danger in modern horror is ideological: films that do not just scare you, but teach you what to believe while your defenses are down.

Horror is uniquely suited to this work. Fear lowers resistance. When an audience's pulse is elevated and their attention is locked on survival, the analytical brain takes a back seat. A film can embed an entire worldview in the space between scares, and the audience will absorb it without ever consciously processing it. The genre's long tradition of social commentary -- from Night of the Living Dead to The Twilight Zone -- has given filmmakers permanent cover. Every sermon can be rebranded as subtext.

Our database contains 103 horror films with complete VirtueVigil Wake Score assessments. The 20 films on this list represent the genre's most aggressive ideological statements -- the ones where progressive messaging is not a garnish. It is the meal. Eight carry the STRONGLY WOKE verdict. Two are WOKE. Six are WOKE LEAN. Four land in BALANCED territory but earn their place through the nature of what they balance.

Ranked from most woke to least woke.

STRONGLY WOKE

#1 (Most Woke): Heretic (2024)

Woke Score: 41.2 • Traditional Score: 13.7 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -27.5 WOKE

Let's not dance around it. Heretic is not a horror film that happens to touch on religion. It is a theological assault on Christianity -- and on all monotheistic faith -- dressed in genre clothing and delivered via Hugh Grant's most charming, murderous performance. The film exists to make one argument: that religious belief is intellectually indefensible, emotionally infantile, and built on a foundation of control that collapses the moment someone asks the right questions. Grant plays a reclusive Englishman who traps two young Mormon missionaries in his house and subjects them to a Socratic interrogation disguised as a game. The craft is undeniable. Grant is mesmerizing. The script is taut. But the film's argument is not presented for debate. It is presented as the conclusion of an intelligent person, and the audience is positioned to nod along. For parents who care what their children absorb about faith, this is the most dangerous horror film in the database -- because it is genuinely good, and genuinely poisonous.

#2: The Bride! (2026)

Woke Score: 34.8 • Traditional Score: 10.4 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -24.4 WOKE

Maggie Gyllenhaal's The Bride! tells you exactly what it is from the very first frame, and it does not care if you approve. Set in 1936 Chicago, the film reimagines the Bride of Frankenstein as a feminist liberation story. The creature is not a monster. She is a woman who refuses to be property. The film explicitly frames marriage as ownership and the bride's awakening as an act of resistance against patriarchal control. Christian Bale's Frankenstein is not a mad scientist. He is a controlling partner. Jessie Buckley's Bride is not a horror victim. She is a revolutionary. The production design is lush, the performances are committed, and the politics are absolute. Gyllenhaal has made a film for audiences who already agree with her, and she makes no effort to persuade anyone else. At -24.4 WOKE, this is one of the most ideologically coherent horror films we have ever scored, and its prestige presentation makes the ideology travel further than a grindhouse feature ever could.

#3: The Substance (2024)

Woke Score: 37.3 • Traditional Score: 13.2 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -24.1 WOKE

Hollywood has always fed on its own. Stars rise, burn bright, and are discarded -- usually on a schedule dictated by age, gender, and the appetite of an industry that treats women as perishable goods. The Substance takes that reality and weaponizes it into one of the most brutal body-horror films ever made. Demi Moore plays an aging star who injects a mysterious drug that creates a younger version of herself (Margaret Qualley), and the two must trade weeks in control. The arrangement does not hold. What follows is a Cronenberg-esque descent into grotesque self-destruction, and the film's argument is not subtle: the beauty industry, the male gaze, and Hollywood's age discrimination are a unified system of violence against women. The body horror is genuinely unsettling, and the craft is exceptional. But the film's feminism is absolute. Every male character is a predator, a consumer, or a coward. The only solidarity is between women. At -24.1, this is a STRONGLY WOKE film that happens to be very well made, and the quality makes the politics harder to dismiss.

#4: Immaculate (2024)

Woke Score: 25.4 • Traditional Score: 3.5 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -21.9 WOKE

Sydney Sweeney spent years developing Immaculate as a vehicle that would let her operate in the horror genre while carrying a message she clearly believed in. The film that emerged -- shot in Italy, dressed in Catholic iconography, structured as Rosemary's Baby filtered through contemporary reproductive rights discourse -- argues that the Catholic Church is not just corrupt but actively monstrous in its treatment of women. Sweeney plays a young American nun who is mysteriously pregnant at an Italian convent. The Church treats her as a miracle. The truth is darker: she was impregnated by the priests using genetic material from a crucifixion relic, and the pregnancy is an experiment in forced breeding dressed as divine intervention. With a traditional score of just 3.5, Immaculate has almost no redemptive traditional content. Its religious imagery is purely aesthetic. Its argument is that institutional religion exists to control female bodies, and that argument is delivered without counterweight or ambiguity.

#5: Leviticus (2026)

Woke Score: 23.8 • Traditional Score: 4.0 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -19.8 WOKE

Leviticus is a competent horror film with a very clear ideological mission: to argue that religious communities opposed to homosexuality are not just wrong, but monstrous. The setup is familiar coming-of-age territory. Naim is the new kid, moving to a small religious town in rural Victoria after his father's death. He discovers his own sexuality in a community that forbids it. Then the genre shifts. The town's religious elders are not merely intolerant. They are supernatural predators who feed on queer teenagers. The metaphor is not hidden. It is the film. What makes Leviticus worth noting is not its quality -- it is a solid but unremarkable horror film -- but its clarity of purpose. It does not use the horror genre to explore a question. It uses the horror genre to deliver a verdict. Religious traditionalism is the monster. Homosexuality is the innocence the monster consumes. That is not subtext. It is the script.

#6: Clown in a Cornfield (2025)

Woke Score: 23.5 • Traditional Score: 4.9 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -18.6 WOKE

Clown in a Cornfield is a competently made slasher with a clear political agenda that it conceals until past the midpoint and then delivers with zero ambiguity. If you enjoy slasher genre mechanics, the first half delivers them. If you care about what the film is actually saying, the second half will concern you. The initial setup is standard: a group of teenagers in a dying Midwestern town, a killer in a clown mask, a series of escalating murders. The twist is that the killer is not a supernatural entity or a revenge-driven individual. The killer is the town's traditionalist faction -- older white residents who have been terrorizing the community's progressive newcomers, and who now escalate from intimidation to murder. The slasher villain is MAGA. The final girl is a progressive activist. The film does not wink at this. It stares you down. The slasher genre has always had political dimensions, but they were usually distributed across the frame. Clown in a Cornfield concentrates them into a single, unambiguous argument: conservative America is the monster under the bed.

#7: Midsommar (2019)

Woke Score: 20.58 • Traditional Score: 2.4 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -18.2 WOKE

Midsommar is a genuinely good film. That is the most important thing to say before everything else, because it shapes how dangerous it is. If Midsommar were a crude feminist horror film, if the cult were obviously evil from the first scene and the protagonist's eventual participation were clearly framed as corruption, the film would be easy to dismiss. But it is not crude and it is not obvious. Ari Aster's daylight horror follows Dani (Florence Pugh), a young woman who has just lost her entire family in a murder-suicide, as she travels with her emotionally absent boyfriend Christian to a Swedish midsummer festival. The boyfriend is the real villain -- not the cult that slowly kills everyone. Christian is neglectful, emotionally manipulative, and incapable of providing the care Dani needs. The cult, by contrast, provides her with community, shared grief, and ultimately a family that sees her suffering and responds. The film's traditional score of 2.4 is among the lowest in our database. By the final frame, the audience has been gently led to cheer for a woman who has chosen a murder cult over her boyfriend, and the film has made that choice feel like triumph. That is extraordinary craft in the service of an ideology that frames female rage as sacred and male inadequacy as the original sin.

#8: MaXXXine (2024)

Woke Score: 31.5 • Traditional Score: 13.6 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -17.9 WOKE

Ti West's X trilogy ends the way it began -- with a woman who refuses to apologize for wanting more. MaXXXine drops Mia Goth's Maxine Minx into 1985 Los Angeles, where the Night Stalker prowls the streets, the Moral Majority screams from every television, and a former porn star claws her way toward Hollywood legitimacy. The film's argument is embedded in its setting: the religious right is the real danger, the porn industry is a workplace like any other, and a woman's right to use her body however she chooses is absolute. The real villain is not the serial killer. It is the conservative moral panic that treats female sexuality as deviance. The film is technically accomplished -- West is a skilled director, Goth is compelling -- but its ideology is as explicit as its violence. Christianity is cast as the enemy of female autonomy. Maxine's ambition is framed as heroism. The final confrontation is not with a monster. It is with a religious fundamentalist who wants to punish her for her choices. At -17.9 WOKE, MaXXXine earns its STRONGLY WOKE verdict through ideological density, not single-issue politics.

WOKE

#9: Presence (2025)

Woke Score: 22.4 • Traditional Score: 8.4 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -14.0 WOKE

Presence is the most technically inventive horror film of early 2025. It is also a quietly progressive film wearing an arthouse horror mask. Steven Soderbergh's latest finds the director in full experiment mode. The film is shot entirely from the ghost's POV: the camera drifts through rooms, watches conversations through doorways, and cannot interact with the living world it observes. What it observes is a family in crisis, and the crisis is organized around a familiar ideological axis. The teenage daughter is the film's moral center -- emotionally intelligent, perceptive, and endangered. The father is distant and professionally absorbed. The mother favors the son, who is revealed to be toxic in ways the family refuses to see. The ghost's allegiance aligns with the daughter. The film's feminism is ambient rather than shouted, but it is everywhere: in the way power distributes across the household, in who is believed and who is not, in what the ghost chooses to protect and what it chooses to let burn. Parents should understand that Presence is not a traditional haunted house film. The haunting is not the point. The family's gender dynamics are.

#10: Get Out (2017)

Woke Score: 16.1 • Traditional Score: 4.0 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -12.1 WOKE

Let's be direct about what Get Out is. It is a very effective horror film built on a very specific political argument: white liberals are the primary threat to Black Americans, they disguise their predation behind progressive language, and the appropriate response is complete distrust of all white relationships. Jordan Peele's directorial debut is a cultural landmark and a genuinely well-constructed thriller. The craft is beyond reproach. But the argument is absolute, and it leaves no room for the possibility that a white person might simply love a Black person without agenda. Every white character is either a predator, a vessel for predation, or a useful tool of predation. The Armitage family does not use racial slurs or wear sheets. They use Obama references and organic food. The horror of the film is not that racists exist. It is that anti-racists are the real racists, and their politeness is the mask. At -12.1 WOKE with a traditional score of just 4.0, this film earned its Best Original Screenplay Oscar. It also earned its place on this list as one of the most ideologically efficient horror films ever made.

WOKE LEAN

#11: The First Omen (2024)

Woke Score: 15.32 • Traditional Score: 7.88 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -7.4 WOKE

The 1976 Omen is one of the great supernatural horror films. Robert Thorn is an American diplomat who discovers his son may be the Antichrist. The film is about a father trying to protect his family from a truth too terrible to accept. The Church figures in it are warnings and helpers. The institution is flawed but fundamentally aligned with good. The First Omen, a prequel set in 1971 Rome, inverts this framework completely. The Church is not a flawed institution that contains good people. It is a conspiracy of men who manufacture evil to preserve their power. An American novitiate discovers that the Catholic Church's most senior figures are orchestrating the birth of the Antichrist -- not as prophecy fulfilled, but as a strategic play to frighten the secularizing world back into the pews. The film's feminism is equally direct: the female body is the site of the Church's violence, and the final girl's arc is a rejection of institutional authority in favor of bodily autonomy. The craft is strong and the atmosphere is genuinely oppressive. But the theology is not. This is a film that uses Catholic aesthetics to argue against Catholic substance, and the argument is not gentle.

#12: The Ugly Stepsister (2025)

Woke Score: 18.12 • Traditional Score: 11.24 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -6.9 WOKE

Emilie Blichfeldt looked at Cinderella and asked the question nobody wanted answered: what would the ugly stepsister's story actually feel like if you told it honestly? The answer, it turns out, involves tapeworms, butcher knives, and more blood than a Dario Argento retrospective. The Ugly Stepsister is a body-horror reimagining of the Cinderella story from the perspective of Elvira, the "ugly" one, who mutilates herself trying to fit the glass slipper. The film is a critique of beauty standards that is not content to be subtext. It is text, delivered through surgical horror and self-mutilation sequences designed to make the audience feel every incision. The male gaze is the villain. The fairy tale is the trap. Female competition is the mechanism that keeps women destroying each other instead of the system that pits them against each other. The film's traditional score of 11.24 reflects genuine craftsmanship and emotional authenticity -- Elvira is not a monster, she is a victim, and the film makes you feel that. But the ideological framework is unmistakable. This is a horror film about how patriarchy makes women destroy themselves, and it does not offer a counterargument.

#13: Forbidden Fruits (2026)

Woke Score: 27.8 • Traditional Score: 21.2 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -6.6 WOKE

There's a store at the Highland Place mall called Free Eden. It sells cupcake-scented candles, charm bracelets, and the kind of overpriced cotton sundress that costs more than your rent. The employees are gorgeous. They have their own slang. They only text boys using emojis. And at some point after closing, they start killing people. Forbidden Fruits is a mall-cult horror film that mixes Gen Z retail satire with genuine genre competence. The cult's philosophy is a pastiche of feminist empowerment rhetoric, wellness culture, and anti-male grievance, and the film walks a careful line between satirizing it and endorsing it. The traditional score of 21.2 is notably high for this list -- the film includes genuine redemptive elements that prevent it from tipping into STRONGLY WOKE territory. But the cult's ideology is presented as seductive for a reason, and the film's interest in female violence as empowerment is not purely anthropological. Parents should know: the horror here is not supernatural. It is social. And the social argument is more complicated than it first appears.

#14: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come (2026)

Woke Score: 16.85 • Traditional Score: 11.2 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.7 WOKE

Ready or Not 2: Here I Come takes the original's eat-the-rich horror-comedy formula and dials it up to a global conspiracy. Whether that's a feature or a bug depends entirely on how you felt about the first film. If you enjoyed Samara Weaving's blood-soaked bride murdering her way through wealthy in-laws in the 2019 original, the sequel delivers more of the same at larger scale. The Le Domas family was one wealthy dynasty. The sequel reveals a network of similar families operating worldwide, and Grace (Weaving) is now hunting them down one by one. The class warfare is explicit. The rich are not just entitled. They are Satanic. The film's politics are openly redistributionist, and its violence is cathartic for audiences who already believe wealth is theft. The traditional score of 11.2 reflects Grace's genuine emotional arc and the film's commitment to her as a character rather than just a vehicle. But the politics are not subtle, and the body count is the argument.

#15: The Crow (2024)

Woke Score: 13.92 • Traditional Score: 8.4 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.5 WOKE

The original Crow is one of those films that should not work as well as it does. Brandon Lee plays a murdered rock musician who comes back from the dead to kill the people who murdered him and his fiancee, guided by a literal crow. It is gothic melodrama with no pretensions to realism. It works because it believes in itself completely. The 2024 remake does not believe in itself. It believes in its politics. The central love story is now between two recovering addicts trying to escape a system that criminalized them. The villains are not just criminals. They are systemic representations of institutional corruption. Eric and Shelly are victims of a world that failed them, and Eric's resurrection is not about love transcending death. It is about refusing to let the system win. The visual style is competent, the action sequences are functional, and the film's heart is in the right place by its own lights. But the gothic romance that made the original work has been replaced by social justice framework, and the result is a Crow film for people who did not like The Crow.

#16: Lisa Frankenstein (2024)

Woke Score: 7.0 • Traditional Score: 2.0 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.0 WOKE

Lisa Frankenstein is Diablo Cody's Jennifer's Body with worse reviews and a better aesthetic. That sentence is both a description and a verdict. Cody's Jennifer's Body (2009) was a horror film about a girl possessed by a demon who ate male victims. Critics dismissed it on release and it was later reclaimed as a feminist cult classic when its target audience grew up and recognized what it was. Lisa Frankenstein follows the same template: misfit female protagonist, supernatural acquisition of power, a trail of male bodies, and a framing that positions the violence as liberation. Kathryn Newton plays Lisa, a high school outcast in 1989 who reanimates a Victorian corpse and discovers that murder is a perfectly reasonable response to adolescent frustration. The film's aesthetic is genuinely charming -- neon-drenched 80s nostalgia filtered through Tim Burton gothic whimsy. But the charm carries a familiar agenda: female violence is cathartic, male targets deserve it, and the only wrong Lisa commits is apologizing for who she is. The woke score of 7.0 is relatively low by this list's standards, but the traditional score of 2.0 tells the real story. There is almost nothing here that reflects traditional values, and the film does not miss them.

BALANCED (But Parents Should Know)

#17: Death of a Unicorn (2025)

Woke Score: 16.9 • Traditional Score: 12.3 • Verdict: BALANCED • Margin: -4.6 WOKE

Yes, Death of a Unicorn has a political lean. It is an anti-capitalist satire wrapped in a creature feature, and it does not try to hide it. The rich people are cartoonishly evil. The young progressive woman is the moral compass. The unicorns are nature's revenge on corporate greed. If you've seen Jurassic Park, Alien, or any movie where a corporation tries to exploit something it doesn't understand and gets eaten for its trouble, you know the template. But Death of a Unicorn has enough self-awareness and enough commitment to its creature-feature mechanics that it plays as entertainment first and sermon second. The traditional score of 12.3 reflects the genuine father-daughter relationship at the film's core -- Paul Rudd and Jenna Ortega have real chemistry, and the film cares about their arc. Parents considering this one should weigh the surface-level gore against the subtext-level politics. The gore is worse than the politics, which is unusual for this list and worth noting.

#18: Us (2019)

Woke Score: 13.14 • Traditional Score: 8.89 • Verdict: BALANCED • Margin: -4.2 WOKE

Jordan Peele's Us has a problem that Get Out didn't have: it's trying to do too many things. Get Out was a scalpel. Us is a Swiss Army knife that doesn't quite close back up properly. The setup is excellent. The Wilson family, headed by Adelaide (Lupita Nyong'o in a genuinely extraordinary dual performance) and her goofball husband Gabe (Winston Duke), arrives at their Santa Cruz beach house for a summer vacation. That night, a family of identical doubles appears in their driveway and begins a home invasion. The doubles are the Tethered -- underground copies of every American, created by a government experiment, abandoned, and now rising to take what they believe is theirs. Peele is trying to say something about America's underclass, about privilege, about the people we step on to live our lives. The allegory is ambitious but the multiple layers compete with each other rather than reinforcing each other, and by the third act the symbolism has become diffuse enough that the film works better as horror than as polemic. Parents should know: Us will scare your teenager. Its politics, unlike Get Out, are sufficiently muddled that they will not land cleanly. That might be a feature, not a bug.

#19: They Will Kill You (2026)

Woke Score: 18.8 • Traditional Score: 14.84 • Verdict: BALANCED • Margin: -4.0 WOKE

They Will Kill You has exactly one thesis and it commits to it with admirable single-mindedness: put Zazie Beetz in a building full of immortal Satanists and watch what happens. It is a simple premise executed with bloody confidence, and for audiences who enjoy that combination, this film mostly delivers. Asia Reaves (Beetz) is an ex-convict who infiltrates The Virgil, a sleek Manhattan high-rise with a quiet history of disappearing housekeepers. She is not there for the job. She is there for answers about what happened to her mother. What she finds is a cult of wealthy elites who have purchased immortality through dark ritual, and what follows is equal parts survival horror and class revenge fantasy. The film's progressive content is present but not dominant: female-led action, anti-elite sentiment, and a protagonist whose moral code is entirely personal. The traditional score of 14.84 reflects genuine competence in genre execution and a protagonist whose motivations are human, not ideological. Parents should know this is a hard-R horror film with significant gore and a Satanic cult framing, but its politics are secondary to its genre work. That puts it in rare company on this list.

#20: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022)

Woke Score: 13.6 • Traditional Score: 10.22 • Verdict: BALANCED • Margin: -3.4 WOKE

Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness is the MCU's most interesting mess. Sam Raimi brings genuine horror filmmaking to a franchise that desperately needed it, Elizabeth Olsen delivers a villain performance for the ages, and the multiverse concept finally gets the unhinged treatment it deserves. It is also a film that introduces a teenage character wearing a pride pin, features an Earth where Captain America is a woman and Captain Marvel is Black, and treats witchcraft as a legitimate power system that produces the most formidable antagonist in MCU history. The woke score of 13.6 reflects representation that operates at the level of design rather than argument -- these elements are present, they are intentional, but they are not the film's thesis. The traditional score of 10.22 reflects Stephen Strange's genuine character arc from arrogance to sacrifice, the film's commitment to its horror set pieces, and the ultimate moral framework that separates Wanda's corruption from Strange's redemption. For parents, this is the safest film on this list ideologically, though its horror elements are intense enough to earn the PG-13 rating honestly. It closes the list as a reminder that a film can contain progressive elements without being consumed by them -- a balance most of the films above it did not attempt.

Methodology

Every score on this list is produced by the VirtueVigil Wake Score (VVWS), a deterministic dual-metric system that rates films on two independent axes: woke content and traditional content. Each axis is scored on Severity (how aggressively the content is presented), Authenticity (how organically it fits the story), and Centrality (how essential it is to the narrative). The margin -- traditional score minus woke score -- produces a locked 7-tier verdict from STRONGLY WOKE to STRONGLY TRADITIONAL. No editorial fudging. No softening for clicks. Just the numbers, consistently applied across 103 horror films and counting.

All 20 films on this list have complete VirtueVigil reviews available at the links provided. Scores and verdicts are current as of August 2026.
